title: Improved quantum sampling methods for molecular simulations
authors: Connor van Rossum, Jeffery Cohn, Sally Shrapnel, Riddhi Gupta
abstract: Quantum-selected configuration interaction (QSCI) methods use a quantum computer to identify dominant electronic configurations in the molecular ground state, while a classical computer diagonalizes the Hamiltonian within the reduced subspace spanned by those configurations. Sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD), a leading QSCI approach, uses iterative classical post-processing to correct noisy quantum measurement to ensure that the corresponding configurations remain physically sensible. In this work, we show that SQD performance can be strongly influenced by uncontrolled growth of the classical diagonalization subspace. When classical resources are not explicitly constrained, classical uniform random sampling can reproduce SQD benchmarks as noise increases the diversity of sampled configurations. We show any fair benchmarking protocol of SQD must explicitly control diagonalization size over unique samples. We then address the problem of efficiently discovering physically relevant, energy-lowering configurations by introducing a measurement protocol based on non-orthogonal configuration interaction (NOCI). By distributing measurements across orbital bases optimized with respect to the molecular Hamiltonian, we obtain improved sample efficiency relative to measurements performed solely in the Hartree--Fock basis. Importantly, these improvements persist even under fixed classical resource budgets, demonstrating that the resulting configurations are of higher quality rather than being more numerous. Under our proposed benchmarking procedure, we establish measurement-basis engineering as a promising route to improving quantum sampling methods for electronic structure.
summary: The paper tackles the inefficiency of current quantum sampling techniques used for molecular electronic structure calculations. It proposes a novel measurement-basis engineering approach called NOCI, which samples measurements across multiple optimized orbital bases rather than just the standard Hartree-Fock basis. This significantly improves the discovery of important electronic configurations while maintaining performance even when classical computational resources are limited.
main_problem: The primary challenge is improving quantum sampling methods for molecular simulations by efficiently identifying physically relevant, energy-lowering electronic configurations.
main_result: Measurement-basis engineering using Non-orthogonal Configuration Interaction (NOCI) shows promise by increasing configurational diversity and alleviating sampling concentration issues, especially when the Hartree-Fock basis is insufficient.
method: The work develops an NOCI measurement protocol that distributes quantum measurements across multiple optimized, non-orthogonal orbital bases to improve sample efficiency over standard methods.
model_or_system: The study focuses on molecular electronic structure simulation, using systems like $	ext{N}_2$ and $	ext{H}_{12}$. The core physics involves diagonalizing the Hamiltonian within a reduced subspace spanned by quantum-selected configurations derived from measurements in various orbital bases.
key_observables: Energy error convergence, configurational diversity (number of unique samples), average orbital occupancies ($o_{\sigma}^{m,\mu}$), and diagonalization subspace size ($d$).
important_parameters: Fixed classical resource budgets, noise levels ($\lambda$), and the choice between orthogonal (HF) vs. non-orthogonal measurement bases.
main_assumptions: The methods do not solve the fundamental challenge of preparing quantum states with high overlap to the true ground state; furthermore, NOCI introduces increased classical cost due to constructing dense Hamiltonian matrices.
figures_summary: Figures compare energy error convergence under varying noise levels and fixed subspace sizes for different sampling strategies (LUCJ vs. Uniform Random Sampling). They also illustrate the workflow comparing standard computational basis measurements versus multi-basis NOCI measurements.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the limitations of current quantum sampling methods like SQD, showing that unconstrained classical resources can mask true performance issues. It then introduces and validates the NOCI measurement protocol by optimizing orbital bases to improve sample efficiency for electronic structure calculations.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses resource constraints in simulating complex molecular Hamiltonians using near-term quantum hardware concepts (quantum sampling), which is highly relevant to AMO physics applications like spectroscopy or reaction dynamics.
